prompt: A man staying in a hotel wakes up during the night to find blood dripping from the ceiling
content:
### The Room Above

At 2:17 in the morning, Martin woke to something cold touching his cheek.

He wiped it away, half asleep, and smelled iron.

A drop of blood shone on his fingertip.

He sat up. Another drop struck the pillow beside him. Then another, landing softly on the sheet.

Martin looked at the ceiling. A dark stain spread above the bed, widening like a bruise.

He called the front desk.

“Probably a pipe,” said the night clerk. His voice was thin with sleep. “I’ll send someone up.”

Martin waited. The drops kept falling.

At last he wrapped a towel around his shoulders and went out into the corridor. The carpet swallowed his footsteps. He found the stairs and climbed one flight to Room 814, directly above his own.

The door stood open.

Inside, the room was identical to his: same gold lamp, same stiff curtains, same framed print of a sailboat. But the bed was made, and the air smelled faintly of dust.

“Hello?” Martin called.

A phone began ringing in the bathroom.

He stepped inside. The receiver hung from the wall, its cord dangling. It rang again.

Martin picked it up.

A woman whispered, “Is he still there?”

“Who?”

“The man in the ceiling.”

The line went dead.

Martin dropped the receiver. In the mirror, behind his reflection, someone stood at the bathroom door.

He turned.

The room was empty.

He hurried back downstairs. The night clerk was waiting at the desk, pale now, with a ring of keys in his hand.

“There’s no Room 814,” the clerk said.

Martin stared at him. “I just came from it.”

The clerk looked toward the elevators. “This hotel has thirteen floors. Room 714 is on the top.”

A soft thud sounded overhead.

The clerk flinched. Martin did too.

Then, from somewhere above them, came the slow scrape of furniture being dragged across a floor.

The clerk lowered his voice. “It happened once before. A guest complained about blood coming through the ceiling. The room above him was empty. In the morning, he checked out.”

“What happened to him?”

The clerk didn’t answer. He was staring at Martin’s shoulder.

A drop of blood slid down the back of Martin’s shirt.

By dawn, the stain on the ceiling had vanished. The hotel manager apologized and offered Martin a free breakfast. Martin packed quickly and left.

Years later, he saw a photograph of the hotel in a newspaper. It had been demolished. During the excavation, workers had found a narrow room bricked up between the seventh and eighth floors.

There was a bed inside, a telephone, and a woman’s small silver bracelet.

The article said nothing about the blood.

prompt: For years , you have taken care of the trash . Today , your trash decides to return the favor .
content:
### The Last Sort

For twenty-six years, you have taken care of the trash at Bellweather House.

You know which tenants forget to tie their bags and which one wraps fish bones in three layers of newspaper. You know that Mr. Alvarez in 4B drinks peach yogurt every morning, because the little cups appear, faithfully, in his recycling. You know the twins on the third floor have outgrown their rain boots, and that someone in 2A is reading a mystery novel a chapter at a time.

You know these things because you look.

You separate what can be separated. You rescue jars with good lids, cardboard before it gets wet, and the occasional chair that only needs tightening. You’ve never thought of this as kindness. It’s just the work.

On Thursday night, rain comes down hard enough to make the building shudder.

You’re in the basement, tying off the last bag, when the lights blink out. A gust of wind slams the alley door. Somewhere above you, a pipe cracks.

Then the water comes.

It rushes beneath the basement door, cold around your shoes. You grab the railing and start up the stairs. Halfway there, a ceiling tile drops onto your shoulder. The railing jerks loose in your hand. You tumble backward and land hard among the bins.

For a moment, all you can do is lie still and listen.

Water pours down the stairs. Your ankle throbs. Your shoulder throbs. Your phone is upstairs, on the kitchen table, where you left it beside a mug of tea.

You try to stand. Your leg refuses.

“Help,” you call.

The storm swallows the word.

A milk jug bumps against your elbow.

You push it away. It bumps you again.

The jug has a blue cap. You remember washing it out this morning and putting it in the recycling, because the new tenant in 5C had left it sticky with juice.

Now it rolls toward the basement stairs.

Behind it comes a second jug, then a third. They bob in the rising water, noses pointed upward. A plastic laundry basket drifts after them. Then a long, frayed clothesline—one you’d pulled from a bag last week and hung on the basement hook.

The line loops itself around the basket handle.

You stare.

A battered umbrella slides across the floor, its crooked tip catching in the handle. The bins begin to knock together. One tips, then another, forming a staggered path through the water.

You have seen strange things in this building. But never the trash making decisions.

The water climbs to your waist.

The laundry basket bumps your knees. The milk jugs press against its sides, wedged in place like bright, empty lungs. The umbrella hooks around your belt.

You understand.

“No,” you say, because it seems polite to object.

The basket tugs.

You grab the clothesline and pull yourself onto the floating pile. It dips beneath you, then rises. The umbrella catches the lowest stair. The whole contraption lurches forward.

You climb.

A can clatters against the radiator, once, twice, again and again. Up above, a window opens. Someone shouts your name.

The basket reaches the top step. The umbrella holds. You drag yourself over the threshold just as the basement door swings open and the water surges through behind you.

Mr. Alvarez is there in his robe. The twins are crying. Their mother has a towel pressed to her mouth.

They lift you onto a chair.

Behind them, in the dark basement, the bins float gently against the ceiling. The milk jugs bob in a patient little cluster. One blue cap turns toward you.

You raise a hand.

The next morning, the rain has stopped. Your ankle is wrapped. Your shoulder is bruised in the shape of the railing.

The tenants leave flowers by your door. Mr. Alvarez brings peach yogurt. The twins bring a drawing of you riding a boat made of rubbish, smiling broadly beneath a yellow umbrella.

You set the drawing on the mantel.

Then you limp to the kitchen and sort the breakfast things: cup, carton, foil lid. Carefully, as always.

At the door, you pause with the bag in your hand.

“Thank you,” you say.

From somewhere below, a bin lid knocks once against the wall.

You smile and take the trash out.

prompt: You are the Sadist who designed Internet Explorer . Write about your thought process .
content:
### The Blue E

I did not set out to become a villain. Villains have lairs. I had a cubicle, a beige monitor, and a mug that said *World’s Okayest Engineer*.

But one afternoon, while everyone else was arguing about browser speed, I stared at a blank design document and thought: *What if the browser were not a window to the internet, but a test of character?*

I began with the loading bar. It would race to ninety-nine percent, pause, and reconsider its life choices. Users would watch it, hopeful. Then it would vanish.

“Why?” my colleague asked.

“Suspense,” I said.

Next came the toolbar. I added a button that looked important but did nothing anyone could easily explain. I made the settings live in three different places, each reached by a different route. I gave the browser a way to remember a password, then made it ask whether it should remember the password every single time.

My colleagues frowned.

I nodded solemnly. “The user must feel involved.”

The little blue E appeared on millions of desktops. People clicked it. It opened. It asked to be the default. They said no. It asked again later, as if we had all simply misunderstood each other.

I watched the support requests arrive and felt something I can only describe as pride—or perhaps indigestion.

Years passed. Faster browsers came and went. The blue E remained, stubborn as a guest who says goodbye from the doorway for forty-five minutes.

Then one day, a user opened it by accident.

I leaned toward my screen.

The browser launched.

The user sighed.

And somewhere, in the deep circuitry of the machine, the loading bar paused at ninety-nine percent.

content:
### The Notes

For eleven months, Mara brought him coffee.

She came at 7:18 every morning, hurrying beneath the station bridge in a navy coat, one hand wrapped around a paper cup. She set it beside the man who sat against the brick pillar, then placed a folded note on top.

At first, he thought the notes were instructions.

*The shelter on Ninth has hot showers.*

*The library opens at nine.*

*It’s going to rain.*

He was grateful for the coffee. The notes he tucked into the pocket of his coat.

His name was Leon. He’d been a cook once, good enough that people used to ask for his gravy recipe. He had a daughter who lived three states away and a talent for letting shame grow until it was larger than any road home. When his apartment disappeared, then his job, then the nerve to call his daughter, he came to the station because it was warm and because trains, at least, always knew where they were going.

Mara kept coming.

One morning, Leon read the note before she’d reached the stairs.

*What did you want to be when you were ten?*

He looked up at her. “A chef.”

She stopped. “Not a fireman?”

“Firemen don’t get to eat their work.”

She laughed, surprised, and the sound seemed to catch her off guard too.

The next day, Leon wrote his answer on the back of a cigarette carton and left it beneath the empty cup.

*I wanted to own a diner. Red stools. Pie in the window.*

After that, the notes changed. They became questions, then stories.

*What’s the best meal you ever made?*

*Chicken and dumplings. My daughter used to lick the bowl.*

*What was her name?*

*June.*

Mara’s notes were in neat blue handwriting. Leon’s replies wandered across whatever paper he could find.

They learned each other slowly. Mara worked in a records office downtown. She took the train each morning and walked the last few blocks. She had taught fourth grade before that. She liked pears but hated pear-flavored candy. She had a husband named Sam who had died two years ago.

That last part arrived on a damp Tuesday, in a note that said only:

*Some mornings I still reach for the other side of the bed.*

Leon folded it carefully and put it in his coat.

The next day he wrote:

*Some mornings I still set out two plates.*

Mara read it. For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Then she sat beside him on the low wall—not too close, not so far away that it looked like she was afraid—and they watched the trains rattle overhead.

After that, she sometimes stayed a minute. Sometimes five. She never asked Leon why he was under the bridge. He never asked why she had started leaving notes.

Then came the morning she didn’t.

At 7:18, Leon watched the stairs. At 7:25, he watched the sidewalk. At 7:40, he told himself he wasn’t watching at all.

The next morning, she came, but she had no coffee. Her coat was buttoned wrong, and her eyes were red.

She put a folded note in his hand.

*Today I can’t manage the train.*

Leon looked up. Mara was gripping the strap of her bag.

“Sit down,” he said.

She did. The bridge shook above them. Leon dug into his coat and found a peppermint, two loose coins, and the cigarette carton with his old diner written on it.

“Bad day?” he asked.

“My mother’s sick. The office is threatening to transfer me. Sam’s birthday was yesterday.” She pressed her palms together. “I don’t know why I’m telling you all this.”

“Because you wrote it down.”

“I didn’t.”

“No,” Leon said. “But you came back.”

Mara stared at the empty place where the coffee usually sat. “I was the one who was supposed to bring something.”

“You did.”

He tapped the note.

She let out a shaky breath. Leon knew that sound. It was the sound a person made when they were trying not to fall apart in public.

He could not fix her mother. He could not get her old job back or give Sam another birthday. But he could sit with her beneath the bridge while the trains went by. So he did.

When the office doors opened, Mara stood. “I should go.”

“Do you have coffee money?”

She gave a small, tired smile. “I think I can afford two.”

The next morning, Leon was waiting with two coffees.

Mara came down the station steps and stopped, surprised.

He offered her the cup. It was too sweet—three sugars, the way she liked it. Beneath the lid, he had tucked a note.

*What did Sam like best?*

Mara read it, then looked at him.

“Your dumplings,” she said. “He was very competitive about them.”

Leon nodded. “I’ll have to make them again someday.”

“Good,” she said, wrapping both hands around the cup.

For a while, they stood together under the bridge, each holding something warm.

prompt: Humanity is at war with an alien race that cleverly uses statistical analysis to predict and anticipate our military actions with incredible accuracy . The only way to defeat them is to be unpredictable .
content:
## The Unmodeled

For eleven months, the Vey had known where humanity would strike.

They knew which ships we would send, which routes we would take, and how long we would wait before retreating. They knew when a commander would risk a few lives to save many, and when she would sacrifice many to save the war. They knew because they had studied every battle we had ever fought—then studied the choices we made when we thought no one was watching.

Their predictions were never perfect.

They were close enough.

At the Battle of Nacre, Admiral Sera Vale watched the Vey fleet arrange itself around the most likely future.

On the tactical screen, red icons crowded the approach to the Nacre Gate. The Vey had left one corridor almost open: a narrow, dangerous passage between two minefields.

“They want us to take it,” said Lieutenant Havel.

“They know we’ll take it,” Vale replied. “It’s the only route that gets the fleet through before the reinforcements arrive.”

The Vey’s prediction engine, the Lattice, had already run the numbers. It had placed its ships exactly where humanity’s best chance would lead us.

Behind Vale, a communications officer spoke up. “Admiral. We’re receiving a civilian distress call. Vey vessel. Unarmed. It’s drifting into the engagement zone.”

The ship appeared on the screen: a long, silver shape tumbling slowly against the stars. Its hull was split open. Heat signatures showed hundreds aboard.

Havel leaned over the console. “Could be bait.”

“It could,” Vale said.

The Lattice would have considered that. It would have weighed the odds that humans would pause to investigate, the odds that we would divert ships to rescue survivors, the odds that mercy was a feint. It would have chosen the response that best protected the Vey.

Vale looked at the corridor. The fleet was ready to go. Her crews had trained for this moment. If they took the passage, they had a chance—perhaps their only chance—to break through.

“Tell the fleet to turn,” she said.

Havel stared at her. “Turn where?”

“To the civilian ship.”

“Admiral, the Vey will know—”

“They’ll know what we’re supposed to do.” Vale stood. “Tell the fleet to turn.”

The order went out.

Across the formation, human ships broke course. They abandoned the narrow corridor and burned toward the crippled vessel. The Vey fleet shifted to meet them. On Vale’s display, probabilities bloomed and vanished: predicted intercepts, likely feints, estimated sacrifice rates.

The Lattice was thinking.

Vale imagined it searching for the advantage hidden in the rescue. A trap. A diversion. A move that made sense if the humans were still trying to win the battle.

She wasn’t.

“Open a channel,” she said.

A Vey voice answered, translated into careful human words. “You are approaching a civilian vessel. Explain your intent.”

“We’re coming to help.”

“Your forces are armed.”

“So are yours.”

A pause. “Your action is tactically irrational.”

Vale glanced at the display. Human ships were taking fire now. One had lost its drive. Another was venting atmosphere from a shattered compartment. They were still moving toward the drifting vessel.

“Maybe,” she said. “But it’s our action.”

The Vey did not fire again.

For a few seconds, nothing moved but the broken ship and the scatter of debris around it. Then the Vey fleet changed formation—not to attack, but to shield the civilians from the crossfire. Their ships turned their guns away from the humans.

That was the opening the Lattice had not predicted.

Not because the Vey were fools. Because every model it had built assumed that the humans’ choices served a human military objective. Even a rescue could be interpreted as a way to win.

Vale’s fleet used the opening to reach the civilian vessel. Rescue craft latched onto its hull. Medics crossed the breach. They carried Vey survivors into human ships, one by one.

No one took prisoners. No one planted charges. No one demanded surrender.

When the last survivor was aboard, Vale ordered the fleet to withdraw.

The Vey let them go.

Two days later, the Vey asked for a ceasefire. The Lattice had offered them hundreds of possible human responses to Nacre. It had not offered this one—not as a serious possibility.

Vale watched the ceasefire signal arrive, small and bright against the dark.

The war had taught humanity to be unpredictable.

At Nacre, they learned something harder: unpredictability wasn’t the same as randomness. It was the freedom to choose a thing that made no sense to the enemy—and to mean it.

prompt: If every country was represented by kids on a playground what would they be doing . ( x-post r/askreddit )
content:
### Recess for the Whole World

At noon, the playground filled with children wearing name tags.

There were so many that the teacher had to bring out extra benches. Each tag had the name of a country written on it, and every country had sent one child.

At first, they did what children do when they meet: they looked around to see what was fun.

Some ran for the swings. Some headed to the climbing frame. A few began drawing elaborate roads in the dirt with sticks. Near the sandbox, two kids were already arguing over whether a sandcastle needed a moat.

“Let’s play tag!” called a child from Brazil.

“Tag has too much running,” said a child from Nepal. “Let’s play something everyone can do.”

“How about a game with rules?” asked the child from Germany.

“How about a game where we make up the rules as we go?” said the child from Jamaica.

“That sounds confusing,” said the child from Japan.

“It might be,” said the child from Jamaica. “But we can try.”

So they tried. The first game lasted less than a minute. Someone got tagged twice, someone else thought they were safe on the slide, and three children ran in different directions shouting different versions of “You’re it!”

They stopped, out of breath.

“We need a better plan,” said the child from Kenya.

They sat in a circle to talk. The circle was lopsided because there were so many of them, and some kids had to sit on the grass. They decided on a game that borrowed a little from everyone: a ball would be passed around, nobody could hold it for more than three seconds, and anyone who dropped it could ask the group to start again.

“Three seconds is too short,” someone said.

“Five,” suggested someone else.

“Four,” said a child from Canada.

They voted. Four won.

Soon the ball was flying from hand to hand. Some passes were neat. Some bounced off knees. Once, the ball rolled under the bench and took a committee of six children to retrieve it.

Nobody won. Nobody seemed to mind.

At the sandbox, the castle had grown enormous. Its builders had used every bucket and spade they could find, and now they faced a problem: the moat was unfinished, and the sand was too dry.

“Water!” called the child from the Maldives.

A little group went to the fountain with cups. Another group carried damp sand back. The child from Iceland made tiny flags from leaves. The child from Egypt shaped a gate. The child from France suggested a tower, and the child from Australia made one that leaned dramatically to the left.

“It’s not supposed to lean,” said the child from France.

“It’s supposed to look interesting,” said the child from Australia.

They decided it could be both.

When the bell rang, the children groaned. They were not finished with the game, the castle, or the argument about whether a leaning tower needed a moat.

“Tomorrow,” someone said.

“Tomorrow,” echoed the others.

They gathered their things. The ball went back into its box. The buckets were stacked. The little leaf flags fluttered above the castle until the wind carried some of them away.

The teacher watched the children file inside, still talking—about rules, and sand, and whose turn it would be next.

The playground was quieter now, but not empty. In the dirt, all those paths crossed and doubled back, making one great, untidy map.

prompt: All doctors must carry a staff . The staff must be hand carved by the doctor , and for every patient a doctor ca n't treat they lose an inch off their staff . When a staff is gone , so is their license .
content:
**The Measure of Mercy**

The first thing Mara carved into her staff was a crooked little moon.

She was twenty-three, newly licensed, and certain that every illness had a name waiting to be found. The staff was ashwood, cut from the tree behind her mother’s house. She shaped it with a pocketknife, smoothing the knots until it fit her palm. Then she carried it into the Hall of Physicians, where the registrar measured it from floor to shoulder.

“Remember,” he said, touching the moon with one finger. “A patient you cannot treat costs you an inch.”

Mara smiled. “Then I’ll learn to treat everyone.”

The registrar did not smile back.

For twelve years, she kept the staff beside her—through fevers and broken bones, through winter coughs and summer births. When she cured someone, the staff stayed as it was. When she failed, the registrar came with a silver blade and cut away an inch.

The first cut came after a child with a blue rash died before dawn. Mara had tried every remedy she knew. She had held the girl’s hand until it went cold.

At the Hall, she stood straight while the registrar marked the ashwood.

“An inch,” he said.

Mara watched the strip fall to the floor.

After that, she learned faster. She read by lamplight, traveled to distant clinics, memorized the names of rare plants and rarer diseases. She became the doctor people asked for when no one else could help.

Still, the staff shortened.

Some patients arrived too late. Some refused the treatment that might save them. Some carried illnesses no book had named. The worst were the ones who came with nothing wrong in their bodies at all, only grief, hunger, or the fear of being left alone. Mara learned that such troubles could be treated, but not always cured.

Each time she failed, the silver blade came.

By the time Mara was forty, the moon she had carved was gone. So were the stars she’d added beside it, and the small river winding beneath them. The staff was shorter than her forearm.

One wet evening, a man staggered into her clinic carrying a child wrapped in a blanket.

“Please,” he said. “She’s stopped breathing.”

Mara took the child. The girl was perhaps seven. Her lips had gone gray, and her chest was still.

“Bring hot water,” Mara told the nurse. “And the bellows.”

She worked until the room was full of steam and lamplight. She pressed, listened, breathed for the child, pressed again. The father stood against the wall with both hands over his mouth.

At last, the girl coughed.

The sound was small and furious. She drew in a breath, then another. Color crept back into her face.

The father sank to his knees.

Mara sat down hard. Her hands were shaking.

In the morning, the registrar arrived. He inspected the staff and frowned.

“This patient was beyond the point of treatment,” he said. “By the rule, you failed her.”

Mara looked at the sleeping child in the next room. “She’s alive.”

“The rule does not measure outcomes. It measures the limits of your skill.”

The registrar set his silver blade against the wood.

Mara caught his wrist.

“I did everything I could.”

“That is not the measure.”

“Then what is?”

The registrar glanced at the staff, as if the answer were carved there. “A physician must know when to surrender.”

Mara released him. “I know when to surrender. I also know when not to.”

The blade fell.

One inch of ashwood struck the floor.

Mara looked at the remnant in her hand. It was scarcely longer than a ruler. She could feel the end of her license approaching—not as a threat, but as a door closing.

That afternoon, a woman came to the clinic with a fever no medicine could break. Mara treated her through the night. By dawn, the woman was dead.

The registrar returned.

This time, Mara did not argue.

The last inch fell.

For a moment, the room was silent. Then the registrar held out his hand.

“Your license,” he said.

Mara placed it in his palm.

He took the short scrap of staff too, but she stopped him.

“That stays.”

“It is no longer a physician’s staff.”

“No,” Mara said. “It’s a piece of wood.”

She carved a handle into it and hung it over the clinic door.

Years passed. Mara stayed in the village, though she was no longer permitted to call herself a doctor. She cleaned wounds, sat with the dying, and taught anyone willing to learn how to boil water and bind a broken arm. The Hall sent letters ordering her to stop. She used them to light the stove.

One spring, the little girl she had saved came back, taller now, carrying a new ashwood staff.

“I made it myself,” the girl said. She had carved a crooked moon near the top.

Mara ran her thumb over the small, uneven shape.

“Are you going to become a doctor?” she asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s all right.”

The girl leaned the staff beside the old one over the door. The two pieces of ashwood rested together: one long and smooth, the other worn down to a stub.

Outside, someone called for help.

The girl reached for her staff.

Mara reached for her coat.

And together they went.

prompt: Build up to something big , but disappoint me in the end
content:
### The Answer

For seventy-three years, the signal came every eleven minutes.

It arrived from a star so distant that, when the first pulse left it, Earth had not yet invented the television. The pulses were too regular to be natural, too deliberate to ignore. They crossed the dark, slipped through the noise of the universe, and tapped at our instruments like someone waiting patiently at a door.

Humanity answered.

We sent numbers, music, photographs, greetings in every language. We sent the sound of rain and the first cry of a newborn. We sent Bach, birdsong, and a recording of a dog barking at the moon.

Then, one winter morning, the signal changed.

The new pulses contained a pattern. The pattern contained a map. The map pointed to a planet in the star’s habitable zone.

The world lost its mind.

Governments formed a single council. Scientists stopped sleeping. Every telescope on Earth turned toward the same small patch of sky. Children learned the star’s name in school. Churches filled. Stock markets froze. People who had never agreed on anything agreed that nothing would ever be the same.

Mara Venn was the first to translate the reply.

She was alone in the control room when the last piece clicked into place. Outside, snow swept across the observatory windows. Inside, the computers hummed, waiting.

Mara read the sentence once.

Then again.

She called the director. He called the council. The council called the president. Within hours, the translation was confirmed by teams on three continents.

The message was simple:

**WE HAVE HEARD YOU. WE WILL ANSWER WHEN READY.**

The world waited.

A year passed. Then two. The signal continued, steady as a heartbeat. Every eleven minutes, it reminded us that someone was out there—and that they had chosen not to speak.

People began to argue about what “when ready” meant. Some believed the visitors were studying us. Others thought they were afraid. A few insisted the message was a warning.

Mara returned to the observatory every winter. She watched the signal arrive, pulse by pulse, and wondered what kind of civilization could take so long to answer.

On the seventy-fourth anniversary, the pattern changed again.

The observatory filled with reporters. The president appeared on a screen. The world watched from phones and living rooms, from crowded squares and quiet hospitals. Mara sat at the central console with the new sequence glowing before her.

She worked through the translation as the countdown reached zero.

The final pulse arrived.

The room went still.

Mara leaned toward the microphone.

“They’ve sent a reply,” she said.

Every person on Earth seemed to hold their breath.

She looked down at the screen.

“They say: ‘We apologize for the delay. Your previous message was received, but it was routed to our promotions folder.’”

prompt: After traveling the world for 15 years to become a master swordsman so he can avenge his family , the protagonist learns his target has already peacefully died in his sleep
content:
### The Last Lesson

For fifteen years, Tomas Vale carried a sword he had not yet earned.

He carried it through the salt deserts of the south, where the wind sanded the names off graves. He carried it into mountain schools where old masters made him practice until his hands split. He carried it across the sea to a city of dueling bells, and beyond that to a country where swords were forbidden but lessons were not.

Everywhere, he learned to fight.

He learned to wait without moving. To hear a man’s breath change before the attack. To strike through rain, through darkness, through fear. In the end, he could cut a falling leaf in two.

He had started the journey at seventeen, with his family’s house burned behind him and the name of the man responsible fixed in his mind: Lord Soren.

Tomas had pictured their meeting a thousand times. In some versions, Soren begged. In others, he laughed. In all of them, Tomas’s sword entered his heart.

When he finally returned to his homeland, he was thirty-two and had a master’s hands.

Soren’s estate stood on a green hill above the town, much as Tomas remembered. Its gates were open. No guards stopped him. At the foot of the steps, a gardener was pruning roses.

“I’ve come for Lord Soren,” Tomas said.

The gardener looked up. “You’re late.”

Tomas’s hand tightened on his sword. “Where is he?”

“Dead.” The gardener set down his shears. “Three weeks now. Died in his sleep.”

The words were so ordinary that Tomas waited for the rest of them. A confession. A challenge. Some cruel twist.

The gardener only wiped his hands on his apron.

“Was he afraid?” Tomas asked.

“No.”

“Did he suffer?”

“No. He went quietly.”

Tomas looked toward the house. Behind one of the windows, a curtain stirred.

He had imagined Soren old and diminished, but alive. He had imagined the justice of seeing the man recognize him. Instead, Soren had slipped away without ever knowing Tomas was coming.

“What happens now?” the gardener asked.

Tomas had no answer.

A young woman came down the steps. She was perhaps twenty, with dark hair pinned carelessly at the back of her head. “You’re the swordsman,” she said.

He turned to her.

“My father told me about your family,” she continued. “Not much. Only that he’d done something unforgivable and that someday someone might come.”

Tomas felt the old heat rise in him. “He killed them.”

“Yes.”

“And you knew?”

“I knew he had blood on his hands. I didn’t know whose until I found his letters.”

She held out a folded sheet. Tomas did not take it.

“He wrote this before he died,” she said. “I thought you should have it.”

At last, Tomas accepted the letter. The paper was thin and faintly scented with smoke.

*I have spent many years hoping the dead would forgive me,* Soren had written. *They have not. I cannot ask the living to do what I have not earned. If you come, I will not hide from you.*

There was no plea. No excuse.

Tomas read the words again, searching for a place to put his anger. The letter offered him none.

He had crossed half the world to become a weapon. He had made his body a promise to the dead. Now the man he meant to kill was beneath the earth, beyond fear, beyond the reach of every lesson Tomas had learned.

“What should I do with this?” he asked.

The young woman glanced at the sword at his hip. “I don’t know.”

It was the first honest thing anyone had said to him all day.

Tomas walked down from the estate and out into the town. He passed the smithy, where a boy hammered a glowing bar of iron, and the old market square where his mother used to buy pears. At the edge of town stood the blackened stones of his family’s house.

Wild grass had grown between them. Someone had planted a small apple tree in the yard.

Tomas knelt and laid his sword beneath it.

For a long time, he sat with his hands empty.

Then, as evening gathered, he stood and began the walk back to town. Not because the past had ended. It hadn’t. Not because he had forgiven Soren. He hadn’t.

But for the first time in fifteen years, there was nowhere he needed to go in order to become a man.

So he went home.

prompt: You know you 're being followed . When you turn around , to catch your stalker you see a familiar face : You .
content:
### The Way Home

You know you’re being followed before you hear the footsteps.

It’s the feeling first: the small tightening between your shoulders, the certainty that the space behind you has become occupied. Then, on the wet pavement, a second set of steps keeps time with yours.

You walk faster. They do too.

The streets are nearly empty. Rain shines on the shop windows, and the traffic lights change for no one. You pass a dark bakery, a closed pharmacy, a bus shelter with a torn timetable. In its glass, you glimpse someone behind you—a figure in a dark coat.

You turn.

Nothing but rain.

You keep walking. The footsteps return.

At the next corner, you spin around so quickly your bag swings against your hip.

This time, someone is there.

A woman stands beneath the streetlamp. Her dark coat is soaked through. Water drips from her hair, and one hand is pressed against her side as if she’s hurt.

Then she steps into the light.

Your face looks back at you.

Not similar. Not a sister, not a stranger with the same eyes. Your face. The tiny notch in your left eyebrow. The faint crease beside your mouth. Even the pale scar on your chin from the time you fell off your bike at nine.

You stop breathing.

The woman looks as frightened as you feel.

“Don’t take the underpass,” she says.

You glance past her, toward the road that leads home. The pedestrian underpass is the quickest way across. You’ve walked through it every night this week.

“Who are you?”

“I’m you.”

“That’s not possible.”

“I know.” She swallows. Her teeth chatter. “You won’t believe me. I didn’t either.”

A car sweeps through the intersection, throwing a sheet of water against the curb. For an instant, the woman’s face disappears behind the spray. When it clears, she’s still there.

You take one step backward.

“Listen,” she says. “The underpass is flooding.”

“How would you know?”

Her eyes flick toward the dark mouth of the tunnel. “Because I went through it.”

A rumble rolls beneath the rain. Not thunder. Lower. Deeper.

The woman grabs your wrist. Her fingers are ice-cold.

“Come on.”

You wrench free. “Don’t touch me.”

She flinches, as if you’ve struck her. Then she turns and runs toward the lit avenue.

You stay where you are.

The rumble comes again. Somewhere ahead, a car horn blares. You look toward the underpass. A ribbon of brown water is spilling from its entrance, spreading over the pavement.

For one long second, you can’t move.

Then the water surges.

You run after the woman.

She’s halfway down the avenue, limping now. You catch up beneath the awning of a closed bank. Together you watch the floodwater burst from the underpass, carrying a traffic cone and a trash bin into the street. It crashes against the curb where you would have been standing.

You turn to her.

She’s trembling, soaked to the skin. A thin red line runs from her temple to her jaw.

“Are you hurt?”

“Not yet,” she says.

The words make your stomach drop.

A siren wails in the distance. You reach for her sleeve, but she steps away.

“Wait. Where are you going?”

“Home.”

“We can go together.”

She gives you a tired, almost tender smile. “We are.”

The streetlamp above you flickers. When it steadies, you’re alone beneath the awning.

At home, you lock the door and stand in the hallway, listening to the rain. You check the mirror. Your face is pale, your hair damp from the weather.

There’s no cut on your temple.

In the morning, the news reports that the underpass flooded just before midnight. Nobody was hurt.

That night, you take the longer route home.

At the corner, you pause. The rain has stopped. Behind you, footsteps cross the pavement, matching your pace.

You keep walking.

prompt: You are an imaginary friend of a serial killer . The person is contemplating another murder , and much to your disbelief , the next victim is you .
content:
### The Last One

I had been with Daniel since he was seven.

Back then, he called me Finch because I was quick and clever and could fit through any crack in the world. I lived beneath his bed, in the hollow behind his wardrobe, in the dark pocket of his coat. I knew the names of all his toy soldiers. I knew which floorboards creaked. I knew how to make him laugh when his father shouted.

For a long time, I thought that was all I was for.

Then Daniel grew up.

He stopped drawing me in the margins of his schoolbooks. He stopped leaving half his sandwich on the windowsill. He stopped talking to me where anyone might hear. But he never stopped seeing me. I sat beside him in lecture halls and on buses, in bars and rented rooms. I watched him become careful. Patient. Good at making people trust him.

I watched him kill.

After the third, I told him he had to stop.

After the sixth, I begged.

After the ninth, I sat across from him at his kitchen table while he wrote a name in his black notebook.

“You can’t keep doing this,” I said.

Daniel capped his pen. “I know.”

The answer startled me. He’d never said that before.

Outside, rain worried at the windows. A clock ticked above the stove. On the table lay a photograph of a woman with bright earrings and a wide, open smile. Daniel had been watching her for weeks.

“Then don’t go,” I said. “Don’t meet her. Don’t even leave the house.”

He looked at the photograph, then at me.

“I’m not going to meet her.”

Relief rose in me so quickly it hurt. “You mean it?”

“Yes.” He folded his hands. “I’ve been thinking. There’s someone else I need to deal with first.”

I frowned. “Who?”

His gaze settled on the empty chair beside mine.

“You.”

For a moment, I laughed. It was the sort of thing I might have said to him when we were children, when we pretended the monsters under his bed had filed a complaint against me.

Daniel didn’t laugh.

“You’re not serious.”

“I’ve been serious for years,” he said. “You’re the one who keeps pretending this is a game.”

I stood up. The kitchen seemed to tilt around me. “You can’t kill me.”

“Can’t I?”

“I’m not real.”

He smiled without warmth. “That’s what you’ve always told me.”

The old confidence drained from me. I knew what I was. I had always known. But knowing I wasn’t real had never felt like the same thing as being helpless.

Daniel opened the drawer beside the sink and took out a small revolver. He set it on the table between us, then turned it—not toward me, exactly, but toward the chair where I sat.

I backed away.

“Put that down.”

“You’ve been in my head since I was seven,” he said. “You tell me what I can’t do. You make me remember things I don’t want to remember.”

“I’m trying to stop you.”

“You’re trying to make me feel guilty.”

“Good.”

His jaw tightened. “You think guilt changes anything?”

“No,” I said. “But it means something in you still knows what you’ve done.”

For a second, I saw the boy he’d been: thin knees, bitten nails, eyes fixed on the dark beneath his bed. The boy who’d whispered, *Stay until morning.*

Then Daniel looked away.

“You were supposed to be my friend,” he said.

“I was.”

He picked up the gun.

I wanted to run, though I had nowhere to go. I wanted to shout for help, though no one could hear me. I wanted to tell him I was afraid, but I couldn’t bear to give him that.

So I said, “If you make me disappear, you’ll still know what you did.”

His hand trembled.

“You can’t shoot a thought,” I said. “You can’t shoot a memory. And you can’t make those people unhappen.”

The clock ticked. Rain slid down the glass.

Daniel lowered the gun.

For a long time, neither of us spoke. Then he reached for the black notebook. He opened it to the last page and stared at the name he’d written there.

The woman in the photograph smiled up at him.

He tore the page out.

Then he picked up the phone.

When the operator answered, Daniel gave his full name. He told her where he was. He told her he wanted to confess to several murders. His voice shook, but he kept talking.

As he spoke, I felt the room loosen around me. The old corners of it—the shadow beneath the table, the narrow gap by the pantry—blurred at their edges.

Daniel glanced toward my chair.

“I know,” he said quietly. “I know you’re not real.”

I had thought those words would hurt more.

When the sirens came, he stayed at the table with both hands visible and the phone set down beside him. The revolver lay untouched between the empty chair and the torn page.

A moment later, the front door opened.

Daniel did not look back at me.

I had been with him since he was seven. I knew every creak in the house, every hiding place, every name he had tried to bury.

I stayed until they led him away.

Then, for the first time in my life, I let him go.

content:
## The Fifth Horseman

The end of the world had a scheduling problem.

“According to the latest prophecy,” Death said, peering over his spectacles, “we require a fifth Horseman.”

War frowned. “Since when?”

“Since the prophecy was revised.”

“By whom?”

Death turned the parchment around. At the bottom, in small print, someone had written: **SUBJECT TO CHANGE.**

Famine leaned over the table. “What’s the fifth one supposed to do?”

“That,” said Pestilence, “is why we’re holding auditions.”

They had rented the Grand Celestial Theater, which was mostly empty except for three cherubs, a suspiciously large number of ravens, and a sign that read:

**THE APOCALYPSE HAS TALENT!**

A skeleton in a sequined jacket bounced onto the stage. “Welcome, doomed souls, to the search for the next Horseman! Our judges are Death, War, Famine, and Pestilence. They’ll be looking for originality, stage presence, and the ability to bring civilization to its knees.”

“Please don’t actually do that,” Death called to the audience. “We haven’t finished the paperwork.”

The first audition was a man calling himself **The Auditor**. He wore a gray suit and carried a briefcase.

“For my act,” he said, “I’ll be explaining the new tax code.”

The audience groaned. Several people fainted. One cherub tried to leave through a window.

War leaned toward the others. “Effective.”

“Too effective,” said Famine. “I’m hungry and I don’t even know why.”

The Auditor received four red Xs and was escorted away by a bailiff who had been waiting outside since Tuesday.

Next came **The Influencer of Pestilence**, a young woman who performed an interpretive dance while spraying the front row with glitter.

“Is the glitter contagious?” Death asked.

“Only emotionally,” she said.

“X,” said Pestilence.

“You can’t X me for being too much like you!”

“I can, and I have.”

Another contestant, **The Great Ennui**, performed a three-hour card trick in which nothing happened. By minute twelve, War was asleep with his sword drawn. Famine had eaten the program. Death admitted he had briefly wondered if his own job might be redundant.

“Remarkable,” he told Ennui. “But we already have winter.”

At last, the skeleton host checked his clipboard. “Our final contestant is… Hope.”

A woman stepped into the spotlight. She wore a patched coat and muddy boots. In one hand she carried a lantern. Its little flame shivered in the enormous dark theater.

War crossed her name off the list. “We’re looking for a Horseman.”

“I know,” Hope said.

“Hope is not an apocalypse,” said Famine.

“Not by itself,” Hope agreed.

Pestilence narrowed her eyes. “What’s your act?”

Hope looked out at the audience. “I help people keep going.”

The Horsemen exchanged glances.

“Is that the whole act?” Death asked.

“No,” Hope said. “That’s the beginning.”

She raised the lantern.

The flame lit the face of a child in the front row. The child had been crying. Now they leaned toward it, curious. Beside them, a woman took the child’s hand. Across the aisle, a man straightened his shoulders. Someone in the back stood up.

The light was small. It didn’t erase the shadows. It didn’t mend the broken walls or put food on the empty tables.

But one by one, the audience began to stand.

War shifted uncomfortably. “What is this?”

“People refusing to give up,” Hope said.

“That’s not very apocalyptic,” Pestilence replied.

“Isn’t it?” Hope turned to her. “You spread sickness. Hope makes people care for one another anyway.”

Pestilence’s expression softened, just slightly. “That is irritating.”

Hope looked at Famine. “You empty the cupboards. Hope makes people share what’s left.”

Famine glanced down at the program crumbs on his lap. “I suppose sharing is inconvenient.”

“And you,” Hope said to War, “can start a hundred battles. Hope can convince people the next one is worth stopping.”

War’s frown deepened. “That’s very inconvenient.”

At last Hope faced Death.

“And you?” he asked.

“You remind everyone that time matters,” she said. “Hope reminds them what to do with it.”

The theater was silent.

Then Death pressed his golden buzzer.

A shower of stars burst overhead. The cherubs cheered. The ravens flew in a frantic circle, as if they’d heard the word *snacks*.

“I vote yes,” Death said. “She understands the stakes.”

War stood. “I hate to admit this, but she has excellent presence.”

“Her act made me feel things,” said Famine. “I’m not certain I approve.”

Pestilence sighed. “Fine. But she’s not allowed to use glitter.”

Hope smiled. “Deal.”

The skeleton host rushed onstage. “We have our fifth Horseman!”

The audience applauded. The five of them stood beneath the glittering lights: Death, War, Famine, Pestilence, and Hope.

The skeleton raised the microphone. “So, Hope—what will your official title be?”

Hope looked at the four Horsemen beside her.

“Not sure,” she said. “Maybe we’ll figure it out together.”

Far above the theater, the clouds parted. Somewhere in the heavens, an enormous book opened by itself. A new line appeared beneath the old prophecy:

**AND THERE SHALL BE A FIFTH.**

The ink paused.

Then it added:

**SHE WILL MAKE THINGS COMPLICATED.**

### The Other Side of Three Minutes

The portal was in the basement of the old observatory, behind a door marked **NO ENTRY** and a stack of broken chairs.

It looked like a standing puddle: black at the edges, silver in the middle, rippling though the air around it was still.

“I’ll go first,” said Mara.

“Why?”

“In case it’s dangerous.”

“And if it is?”

“Then you’ll know not to follow.”

“That’s not a great plan.”

“It’s a plan.”

She grinned, the same fearless grin she’d had since we were ten, and stepped through.

The silver folded around her. Then it was gone.

I waited three minutes. Maybe four. I called her name. I tapped the wall. I considered getting help, then pictured trying to explain a magic doorway to the police.

Finally, I stepped through.

The smell hit first: smoke, mud, and something metallic. I stumbled onto a hillside beneath a bruised purple sky. Below me stretched a battlefield so enormous I couldn’t see its end. Broken wagons and splintered spears littered the churned earth. Fires smoldered in the wreckage. Here and there, people moved among the fallen, calling for survivors.

A man in battered armor lay against a shattered wheel. One sleeve was dark with blood. He lifted his head when he saw me.

“About time,” he said.

I stared at him. “What?”

“The captain said there’d be two.” His eyes flicked past me, toward the air where the portal had vanished. “You’re the second.”

“Where is she?”

He pointed across the field.

At the far end, a line of soldiers stood beneath a torn blue banner. In front of them was a woman with a sword in one hand and a dented helmet tucked under the other arm.

“Mara,” I breathed.

She turned.

For a moment, she didn’t move. Then she ran.

I ran too. We met halfway across the broken ground, and she grabbed me so hard I nearly fell.

“You came,” she said into my shoulder.

“Of course I came.”

She leaned back to look at me. There was a thin scar along her jaw that hadn’t been there in the basement. Her hair was shorter, threaded with a few pale strands. She looked older—not old, exactly, but like someone who had lived through a great deal.

“How long?” I asked.

Mara glanced toward the sky, then back at me.

“Nine years.”

My mouth opened. Nothing came out.

“The portal shut behind me,” she said. “I couldn’t get home. I thought it might open again someday.” She smiled, tired and shaky. “I told everyone my best friend would follow.”

Behind us, the wounded man gave a groan.

Mara’s smile vanished. She turned and raised her sword, calling for a medic. Around us, survivors were lifting the fallen, passing water, and gathering beneath the blue banner.
